title: The abandoned Glasgow 'mental asylum' dating back to 1896 that former staff claim is haunted
excerpt: The old asylum has a long history of ghost stories, with former staff members even claiming to have experienced paranormal experiences while they worked there.
content:
The old asylum has a long history of ghost stories, with former staff members even claiming to have experienced paranormal experiences while they worked there.

14:25, 11 Oct 2026

Lying abandoned since its closure in 1996, Gartloch Hospital has been a fixture in Glasgow's east end for well over a century. The historical Category A listed building, which formerly served as a psychiatric hospital, was open for 100 years before it was shut down.

‌

‌

The building first opened its doors as the Gartloch District Asylum in 1896, with a maximum capacity of 830 patients. But today, it is known as one of the most haunted locations in Glasgow.

‌

The old asylum has a long history of ghost stories and urban legends surrounding it with former staff members even claiming to have experienced paranormal experiences while they worked there, according to Spooky Isles.

‌

While much of the site where the asylum operated has now been redeveloped, the main administration block and core historic structures remain. These can be found on Gartloch Road near the village of Gartcosh, which is a short drive from the popular outdoor shopping centre, The Glasgow Fort.

The City of Glasgow first bought the Gartloch Estate with plans to build a hospital back in 1889, before officially laying the foundation stone in 1892, the Record reports.

‌

The facility was built by Robert Douglas Sandilands and John Thomson with the latter being the son of famed Scottish architect Alexander 'Greek' Thomson. This came about after the pair won a competition to design what was at the time known as the City of Glasgow District Asylum.

After its closure, many of the surrounding buildings were either converted into residential properties or demolished to make way for Gartloch Village.

However, the Victorian-era towers still loom large, despite countless windows having caved in and the structure now being beyond any hope of restoration.

‌

The Gartloch hospital grounds also previously housed a tuberculosis sanatorium which was created to tackle what was once the leading cause of death across the western world.

Patients were moved out during the Second World War to accommodate an emergency centre, with temporary huts erected on the grounds to serve as additional wards.

David Tennant fans may also recognise the building from a particularly haunting 90s drama focused on a hospital radio station.

‌

The BBC series Takin' Over the Asylum, released in 1993, used Gartloch's exterior as the fictional St Jude's Asylum.

Since Gartloch closed its doors, speculation about redevelopment has been rife across the city, and in 2019 a proposal to transform the main building into 12 flats received approval.

Before developers arrived on site, several adventurous urban explorers entered the abandoned building and shared footage of their adventures online.

However, entering the building is not recommended, and is currently not possible due to the ongoing renovation works.
